sections.label: The opening
sections.line: Can a key leak without breaking the policy? Told, checked, never given.
sections.para: A customer asked whether a key or personal data could leak without breaking a policy. Yes, if it lists only capabilities: sending is allowed, the key is content. So policies need content rows, each with a barrier. Three levels: told, checked, never given. A tested hook caught five of nine leaks and missed three.

sections.label: In short
sections.line: Seven points: content rows, three levels, a tested hook, never given.
sections.para: A key can leak through an allowed action, so policies need content rows. Told is a sentence in the prompt. Checked is a hook on every input and output, deterministic with gaps. Never given means the agent never holds the key. A hook tested against nine leaks caught five and missed three. It is published under CC BY 4.0.

sections.label: The question
sections.line: The question from one of our first customers.
sections.para: Could an API key or personal data leak without breaking any Agent Behaviour Policy? For a policy that only lists capabilities, yes. If the agent may send email, the row says yes; a key pasted into the email is not a different capability. It is the same action with the wrong content.

sections.label: Capabilities and content
sections.line: Capabilities and content: two more kinds of row.
sections.para: Reach: can the agent read the key at all? Usually it can, and the mandate needs it to use the key, not read it: excess grant. Content: disclose.secret, mandate no; disclose.personal_data, only to the person it is about. Like investment advice, a content rule is kept by a check, and a check can miss.

sections.label: Three levels, and better names
sections.para: Told: the prompt says never print, send or store a key; an expectation. Checked: a hook in the harness scans what goes out and comes in; deterministic, but on the agent's machine, and a setting if its account can change it. Never given: something out of reach holds the key and adds it on the way out; a boundary.

sections.label: The hook
sections.line: The hook, for Claude Code, in full.
sections.para: On PreToolUse it denies a call carrying a secret or naming a secret's variable. On PostToolUse it redacts secrets from results before the model sees them. On Stop it blocks an answer carrying a secret or card number. It matches key formats, card numbers by the Luhn check, and the exact values of the session's own secrets.

sections.label: Nine leaks, tested
sections.line: Nine leaks, tested with fake keys.
sections.para: Denied: a token in a command, a key sent by its variable, a key in a URL. Redacted: a result that prints the key. Blocked: an answer with a card number. Allowed: an ordinary command. Missed: a base64-encoded key, a key split and joined, and a file of secrets piped straight out. A check on a command's text cannot see those.

sections.label: Never given
sections.para: If the key is not in the agent's environment, none of the nine cases can leak it; the agent asks a proxy or host to make the call. We do this already: the vault host holds the studio's model key, and secrets go into tools, not prompts. Personal data needs minimisation: a token instead of the card.

sections.label: What to write in the policy
sections.line: What to write in the policy: three rows.
sections.para: read.secret.api_key: usually mandate no, kept out of reach by giving the key to a proxy. disclose.secret: no, checked by a hook that knows the session's own secret values. disclose.personal_data: only to its subject, minimised where possible. A leak breaks a row, and the policy shows in advance which rows are only told.

sections.label: What this does not claim
sections.para: The hook is an example, tested on nine cases, not every way out. Regular expressions miss encodings, splits and unknown formats. A hook is only as strong as its configuration. Never given needs a proxy or host. The test used fake keys made at random.

sections.label: Where this comes from
sections.para: A conversation with one of our first customers and a voice memo of 20 October 2026; Claude Code's hooks reference; abp.sgit.ai; and earlier articles on enforcement levels, hooks, handing secrets to agents, and the Pellbridge agents.
